prompt.adult: Psalm 114 remembers the sea that fled and the river that turned back. In 114:4, how did the mountains skip?
prompt.child: Psalm 114 says that when God led His people, even the mountains jumped. How did they skip?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 114:4, how did the mountains skip?

verses.text: The mountains skipped like rams, The little hills like lambs.

explanation.child: Look at the start of verse 4.
explanation.teen: 114:4 has two lines: the mountains and then the little hills. Read the first.
explanation.older: It closes the first line of 114:4.

teaching.extended_explanation: 114:3 says the sea saw it and fled. 114:6 later turns to the mountains and the little hills and asks them about it.

prompt.adult: In 121:4, what does He who keeps Israel never do?
prompt.child: Psalm 121 says God watches over Israel all the time. What does He never do?
prompt.teen: Psalm 121:4: “Behold, He who keeps Israel Shall neither” do what?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 121:4, what will Israel’s keeper never do?

verses.text: He will not allow your foot to be moved; He who keeps you will not slumber.
Behold, He who keeps Israel Shall neither slumber nor sleep.

explanation.child: Look at the last words of verse 4.
explanation.teen: 121:4 names Israel’s keeper and then what He never does. Read the end.

teaching.extended_explanation: 121:3 says He will not allow your foot to be moved. 121:5 goes on: “The LORD is your keeper; The LORD is your shade at your right hand.”

prompt.adult: In 118:22, what has the stone which the builders rejected become?
prompt.child: The builders threw away a stone, but it became the most important stone. What did it become?
prompt.teen: Psalm 118:22: “The stone which the builders rejected Has become” what?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 118:22, what has the rejected stone become?

verses.text: The stone which the builders rejected Has become the chief cornerstone.
This was the LORD’s doing; It is marvelous in our eyes.

explanation.child: Look at the end of verse 22.
explanation.teen: 118:22 has two lines: the rejection and what followed. Read the second.

teaching.extended_explanation: 118:23 says, “This was the LORD’s doing; It is marvelous in our eyes.” 118:24 follows with “This is the day the LORD has made.”
teaching.takeaway: The rejected stone “Has become the chief cornerstone.”

prompt.adult: “Bring back our captivity, O LORD.” In 126:5, what shall those who sow in tears do?
prompt.child: Psalm 126 talks about people who plant with tears. What will happen to them later?
prompt.teen: Psalm 126:5: “Those who sow in tears Shall ___.” What fills the blank?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 126:5, what awaits those who sow in tears?

verses.text: Bring back our captivity, O LORD, As the streams in the South.
Those who sow in tears Shall reap in joy.

explanation.child: Look at the end of verse 5.
explanation.teen: 126:5 sets two lines side by side. Read the second.

teaching.extended_explanation: 126:4 asks the LORD to bring back their captivity “As the streams in the South.” 126:5 sets the time of sowing beside the time that follows it.
teaching.takeaway: Those who sow in tears “Shall reap in joy.”

prompt.adult: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brethren to dwell together in unity!” In 133:3, unity is like the dew of where?
prompt.child: Psalm 133 says living together in peace is like dew. The dew of which place?
prompt.teen: Psalm 133:3: “It is like the dew of ___, Descending upon the mountains of Zion.” What fills the blank?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 133:3, the dew of which place pictures unity?

verses.text: Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brethren to dwell together in unity!
It is like the precious oil upon the head, Running down on the beard, The beard of Aaron, Running down on the edge of his garments.
It is like the dew of Hermon, Descending upon the mountains of Zion; For there the LORD commanded the blessing— Life forevermore.

explanation.child: Look at the start of verse 3.
explanation.teen: 133:2 gives one picture, oil; 133:3 gives a second. Read it.

teaching.extended_explanation: 133:2 compares unity to the precious oil running down on the beard of Aaron. 133:3 ends: “For there the LORD commanded the blessing— Life forevermore.”
teaching.takeaway: It is like the dew of Hermon.

prompt.adult: In 123:2 our eyes look to the LORD as servants look to the hand of their masters. In 130:6, the psalmist waits more than those who watch for what?
prompt.child: Psalm 130 says the writer waits for God even more than some people wait and watch. What are they watching for?
prompt.teen: Psalm 130:6: “More than those who watch for” what?
prompt.older: According to Psalm 130:6, the psalmist’s soul waits more than watchers wait for what?

verses.text: Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hand of their masters, As the eyes of a maid to the hand of her mistress, So our eyes look to the LORD our God, Until He has mercy on us.
My soul waits for the Lord More than those who watch for the morning— Yes, more than those who watch for the morning.

explanation.child: Look at the last words of verse 6.
explanation.teen: 123:2 is the setting; 130:6 makes its comparison twice. Read the end of either line.

teaching.extended_explanation: 123:2 pictures eyes looking to the LORD until He has mercy. 130:6 repeats its line for emphasis.
teaching.takeaway: He waits more than those who watch for the morning.

prompt.adult: Psalm 118:8 says it is better to trust in the LORD than in man. In 115:9, Israel is told to trust in the LORD, for He is their help and what?
prompt.child: Psalm 115 tells Israel to trust God. It says God is their help and something else. What?
prompt.teen: Psalm 115:9: “O Israel, trust in the LORD; He is their help and” what?
prompt.older: Psalm 118:8 praises trust in the LORD. According to 115:9, the LORD is Israel’s help and what?

verses.text: O Israel, trust in the LORD; He is their help and their shield.
It is better to trust in the LORD Than to put confidence in man.

explanation.child: Look at the last words of Psalm 115:9.
explanation.teen: 118:8 is the setting; 115:9 names two things the LORD is. Read the second.

teaching.extended_explanation: 118:8 compares trusting in the LORD with putting confidence in man. 115:10-11 repeat the line from 115:9 for the house of Aaron and for those who fear the LORD.
teaching.takeaway: He is “their help and their shield.”

prompt.adult: In 129:4 the LORD has cut in pieces the cords of the wicked. In 124:7, from what has our soul escaped as a bird?
prompt.child: Psalm 124 says God’s people got free like a bird. What did the bird escape from?
prompt.teen: Psalm 124:7: “Our soul has escaped as a bird from” what?
prompt.older: Psalm 129:4 tells of cords cut. According to 124:7, from what did the soul escape like a bird?

verses.text: Our soul has escaped as a bird from the snare of the fowlers; The snare is broken, and we have escaped.
The LORD is righteous; He has cut in pieces the cords of the wicked.

explanation.child: Look at the start of Psalm 124:7.
explanation.teen: 129:4 is the setting; 124:7 says what the bird escaped. Read its first line.
explanation.older: It ends the first line of 124:7.

teaching.extended_explanation: 124:6 blesses the LORD, who has not given us as prey to their teeth. 129:4 opens with “The LORD is righteous.”
teaching.takeaway: Our soul escaped “as a bird from the snare of the fowlers.”
